keep: The idea is named in one line up front (3/8 and 6/16 of an inch are the same mark: one number, two names) and the rule is stated in words before any arithmetic: cut every piece into the same number of smaller pieces and both numerals change but the mark does not move.

One fully worked example computed from the rule: one eighth 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125, three of them 0.375; one sixteenth 1 ÷ 16 = 0.0625, six of them 0.375; then 12/32 the same way. The why (the piece shrinks by the factor the count grows, so the two cancel) is in words and the whatAmILookingAt states it as the rule the readouts compute.
Two misconceptions shown failing with numbers: the whole-number habit ([^17], 6/16 looks like more) and adding the same number to top and bottom (4/9 reaches about 0.444 inches, past the mark).

The brief names the cause (cut each eighth into more pieces) and the effect (the pointer stays at 0.375 while the name changes), one control, outputs computable from pieces in inch = 8 × slider, pieces counted = 3 × slider, place = counted ÷ in inch.

Analogy from Dan's trade (2.3 kW = 2300 W: a smaller unit, a thousand times more of them, the same load) reproduces the result, and differs from the clamp meter, the three-phase board and the series lamps; breaks named (hidden bottom number, fixed steps of ten).

Names match i1-i3: bottom/top number, the whole, piece, pointer, filled run, label above it, the 750 mm mark; one new term, [[equivalent fractions]]; every [^n] is on words its quote supports and sources lists exactly those cited; the closing takeaway is all bold and footnoted.
fix: Talking about the lesson: 'and that is what this lesson is about' at the end of the first paragraph. Cut it.
Shape: six paragraphs in explain. Merge the one-sentence 'same whole' paragraph into the habits paragraph, so the explain is five, and the takeaway stands last.
The new term equivalent fractions is named but never used again in this lesson; use it once in practice so the name is earned twice before i5 and i6 lean on it.

False absolute in the common mistakes: 'Adding the same number to the top and the bottom ... has moved' is stated as if adding always moves the mark, but a fraction exactly equal to 1 (3/3 to 4/4) stays at 1. Say the mark moves unless the fraction is already exactly 1; keep 'never add' as the rule of thumb, since adding is not a way to rename.
'the shape of this rule is no shape at all' is cute rather than plain; say the row is flat because nothing about the length is changing.

'simplest form' is a textbook term dropped in with 'textbooks add that', fine, but the sentence before it ('the one you would normally say and write') is a claim about habit, not maths; shorten to the plain fact: the name with the smallest numbers is the one usually written, and textbooks call it the simplest form.

whatAmILookingAt: 'with yours picked out' should be 'with the dot for your current setting picked out', as i3 words it; and say in one clause why the readout at setting 1 shows 8 pieces and 3 counted, so every readout is explained at the opening setting.

Practice worked example: 'each quarter is 250 of the millimetre pieces' needs the cut said plainly: cut each quarter into 250 pieces of 1 mm, multiplying top and bottom by 250, so the step matches the lesson's rule rather than reading as a new method.
